title: Natural Language To SQL, Guarded Execution
description: Natural language to SQL using locally hosted models: schema-aware prompting, read-only database roles, benchmark notebooks measuring accuracy, and the security architecture preventing arbitrary query execution.

lines.text: Operations manager types: show me last month's failed payments by provider.
Behind the scenes, a language model writes SQL against a production PostgreSQL database.
Read-only, I hope.
Exactly. And the answer determines whether this is a productivity tool or a breach waiting to happen.
The model writes SQL. That SQL executes against real payment data in PostgreSQL.
What could go wrong?
DROP TABLE customers. Or UPDATE payments SET amount equals zero. Or a JOIN that silently returns wrong revenue figures.

sections.title: How do you let a model write SQL safely?

lines.text: Chat interface converts natural language to SQL using locally hosted open-source models.
Docker services: web UI, Qwen model server for SQL generation, PostgreSQL.
Everything local. Four gigabytes disk for weights. No cloud dependency.
Why local? Cloud is better.
Sensitive data stays on network. No per-query cost. No vendor lock-in for internal tools.
Trade-off acknowledged: Qwen three-billion generates weaker SQL than GPT-four. Benchmarks quantify exactly how much.
Project uses Qwen two-point-five models served locally via Ollama or vLLM.
Two sizes tested: zero-point-five-billion for speed and three-billion for accuracy.
PostgreSQL runs in Docker alongside the model server and web UI. Three containers total.
Why not just use GPT-four via API?
Sensitive payment data must stay on network. No per-query API cost. No vendor dependency for internal tooling.
Model needs table definitions, column names, relationships in the prompt to generate valid SQL.
Schema representation matters. Full DDL for six tables fits. Larger schemas need selective inclusion.
Execution guardrails operate at connection level. PostgreSQL role gets SELECT privilege only, no INSERT UPDATE DELETE DROP.
Even destructive generated queries fail at database level.
Query timeout prevents runaway scans blocking other users.
Syntactically valid but semantically wrong SQL? Harder problem.
Syntax errors get caught. Semantic errors return plausible-looking wrong numbers. Benchmarks compare against hand-written references on known questions.
Schema-aware prompting injects table definitions, column names, types, and relationships into every request.
Six tables in demo schema: api_gateway logs, auth service users, payment transactions, billing accounts, notification events, reporting jobs.
Full DDL for six tables fits comfortably in prompt context. Larger schemas need selective inclusion based on query relevance.
Few-shot examples teach the model expected SQL style and common patterns.
Execution safety starts at connection level. PostgreSQL role granted SELECT privilege only.
Even if model generates DROP TABLE, database refuses with permission denied error.
Query timeout set to thirty seconds prevents runaway analytical scans blocking other users.
Secondary model generates natural-language summary of results. Zero-point-five-billion variant sufficient for summarization.
Question enters chat. System constructs prompt: schema, few-shot examples, question.
Qwen generates SELECT provider, COUNT FROM payments WHERE status failed AND date range GROUP BY provider.
Application validates syntax, enforces timeout, executes read-only.
Results return as table. Secondary smaller model summarizes in plain English.
Benchmark notebook runs twenty reference questions through both zero-point-five-billion and three-billion-parameter models.
Measures execution accuracy and latency. Larger model substantially more accurate. Smaller faster but more logical errors.
Concrete example from benchmark notebook.
Question: how many payments failed per provider in January twenty-twenty-six?
Reference SQL written by hand: SELECT provider, COUNT star FROM payments WHERE status equals failed AND created_at BETWEEN January first and January thirty-first GROUP BY provider.
Qwen three-billion generates nearly identical SQL. Execution result matches reference exactly.
Qwen zero-point-five-billion generates syntactically valid query but joins on wrong column, returning inflated count.
Syntactically correct, semantically wrong. This is the hardest error class to catch automatically.
Benchmark measures execution accuracy: does query result match reference result on same database?
Twenty reference questions cover simple aggregations, grouped counts, multi-table joins, and date-range filters.
Three-billion model achieves substantially higher execution accuracy than zero-point-five-billion. Exact percentages documented in notebook.
Model footprint: four gigabytes quantized to four-bit for three-billion variant.
Apple M2 inference: one to three seconds per query depending complexity.
PostgreSQL varies: simple aggregation milliseconds, reporting joins seconds.
Execution accuracy meaningful for prototyping, not production-grade without human verification.
Docker Compose startup under two minutes including first model load.
Performance and resource numbers.
Model disk footprint: four gigabytes quantized Qwen three-billion. Zero-point-five-billion fits in one gigabyte.
Apple M2 inference latency: one to three seconds per query for three-billion model.
PostgreSQL query time: milliseconds for indexed aggregations, seconds for unindexed analytical joins.
Docker Compose cold start including model loading: under two minutes on M2 MacBook Air.
Memory usage: three-billion model consumes roughly four gigabytes RAM during inference.
Zero infrastructure cost beyond the laptop running Docker. No API keys required.
Question enters. Schema-aware prompt constructs. Local Qwen generates SQL. Application validates syntax and timeout.
Read-only role executes. Results return as data. Secondary model summarizes. Both render in UI.
Everything Docker Compose locally. No data leaves machine.
Complete request lifecycle.
Question typed in chat interface. Backend constructs schema-aware prompt with relevant table definitions and few-shot examples.
Local Qwen model generates SQL query text. Application validates basic syntax and enforces timeout wrapper.
Read-only PostgreSQL role executes query. Results return as structured rows.
Secondary model summarizes results in plain English alongside the raw table.
Everything runs locally in three Docker containers. No external API dependency.
Hallucinated column name. PostgreSQL undefined column error. Fix: include descriptions, retry with error feedback.
Valid syntax wrong JOIN logic returns plausible wrong numbers. Benchmark mismatch catches on known questions. Novel patterns need human review.
Reporting queries lock tables during peak traffic. Route analytics to read replica, never primary.
Pending: who approves accessible tables? Row-level security requirements? Schema changes stale prompts? Audit trail for generated queries?
Additional failure modes from real usage.
Model hallucinates column name that sounds plausible but does not exist in schema.
Signal: PostgreSQL undefined column error. Fix include column comments in prompt, retry with error message appended.
Model writes correct-looking JOIN but on non-key column, producing Cartesian product explosion.
Signal: result set unexpectedly large or query timeout triggered. Fix row-count sanity checks on results.
Schema changes after deployment. Column renamed, breaking cached prompts referencing stale names.
Signal: sudden spike in undefined column errors. Fix dynamic schema introspection rather than hardcoded DDL strings.
Pending: who approves accessible tables? Row-level security requirements? Audit logging for generated queries? Schema change notification process?
Can your connection execute DROP TABLE? If yes fix first.
Do you benchmark against known questions or eyeball output?
When schema changes, how does system know its prompts are stale?
Fourth: if you removed all LLM components, would the read-only database role still protect you from accidental destructive commands?
Defense in depth means the database guardrail survives independently of the AI guardrail.
Fifth: can a non-technical user tell when the generated SQL is likely wrong versus probably right?
Self-test: model joins payments to customers on email instead of customer ID. What kind of error and how catch it?
That wraps the series. Search, support, clinical, voice, recommendation, extraction, validation, scheduling, pipelines, and SQL.
Common thread: define good precisely, build smallest honest loop, measure failures, keep docs equal to reality.
Same discipline, every domain.
That is forward-deployed engineering.
What about letting the model write INSERT statements for data entry automation?
Different risk profile entirely. Write access requires transaction rollback, audit trails, and much stricter validation. Separate project.
